units.title: Unit 29 — Film and book reviews
learningObjectives: Interpret film and book reviews using collocations about plot, atmosphere, suspense and originality.
Describe performers, casting, critical reception and artistic success in a register-appropriate way.
Contrast positive reviews with strongly negative criticism and recognise unnatural word partners.

items.example: The documentary tells the story of a violinist who built a school in her village.
items.note: Tell the story of introduces the subject or central narrative of a film or book.

items.example: A rare manuscript vanished under mysterious circumstances shortly before the exhibition.
items.note: This phrase suggests that the reasons for an event remain unexplained.

items.example: The suspense builds up as the detective approaches the abandoned station.
items.note: Build up describes tension gradually becoming more intense, not appearing all at once.

items.word: set off a chain of events
items.example: A misplaced letter sets off a chain of events that changes three families' lives.
items.note: Set off a chain of events indicates that one occurrence triggers several linked consequences.

items.pt: filme envolvente que prende a atenção
items.example: Her debut is a gripping film about survival in a remote coastal town.
items.note: Gripping is a strong positive description of a story that holds the audience's attention.

items.example: The production shows startling originality in its use of sound and lighting.
items.note: Startling adds an element of unexpected surprise to the originality of a work.

items.example: Casting the entire play with first-time performers was a bold experiment.
items.note: Bold experiment praises or questions a creative risk rather than a routine choice.

items.example: Maya was cast in the role of a scientist investigating a vanished expedition.
items.note: Be cast in the role of is a conventional passive construction for assigning an acting part.

items.example: Even in a minor scene, the accomplished actor makes every gesture believable.
items.note: Accomplished describes a performer with highly developed skill, not simply somebody famous.

items.example: Despite repeated technical delays, she remained a consummate professional throughout filming.
items.note: Consummate is formal praise for someone who demonstrates complete professional expertise.

items.pt: realizar algo difícil com grande êxito
items.example: The young cast faced a difficult script but managed to carry it off brilliantly.
items.note: Carry something off means succeed at something challenging; brilliantly intensifies the praise.

items.example: A star-studded cast helped the historical drama attract international attention.
items.note: Star-studded means featuring many well-known performers, not necessarily high artistic quality.

items.example: The closing scene offered a dazzling display of talent from the whole ensemble.
items.note: A dazzling display is an exceptionally impressive demonstration of an ability.

items.example: The memoir traces an extraordinary series of events during one turbulent winter.
items.note: Series of events refers to successive occurrences; extraordinary marks them as unusual.

items.example: The stage adaptation was spectacularly successful despite its modest budget.
items.note: Spectacularly modifies successful to describe a strikingly high degree of success.

items.example: The independent film received glowing reviews after its festival premiere.
items.note: Glowing reviews are strongly favourable critical assessments, not just numerous reviews.

items.example: The outdoor screening was an unmitigated disaster after the sound system failed.
items.note: Unmitigated is emphatically negative and signals a disaster without redeeming features.

items.example: Her visual style was strongly influenced by early experimental photography.
items.note: Strongly influenced by describes a substantial effect on someone's work or ideas.

items.example: The novelist was heavily influenced by oral storytelling traditions.
items.note: Heavily is a natural alternative to strongly with influenced; highly influenced is not usual.

items.example: The theme music returns quietly during the final scene.
items.note: Theme music is the recognisable musical material associated with a film or programme.

items.example: I highly recommend the audio edition to anyone who enjoys historical fiction.
items.note: Highly recommend conveys a strong endorsement; spectacularly recommend is not idiomatic.

items.example: We thoroughly recommend this short novel for its sharp dialogue.
items.note: Thoroughly is another natural intensifier with recommend, with the sense of wholehearted approval.

items.example: I could hardly bear the suspense while the rescue team searched the cave.
items.note: Bear the suspense means tolerate the tension of waiting for a story's outcome.

items.pt: ter uma opinião muito positiva sobre
items.example: Several reviewers think highly of the director's recent work.
items.note: Think highly of means hold a favourable opinion; it contrasts with the incorrect high reputation.

items.example: The sequel was a dismal failure even among devoted fans of the series.
items.note: Dismal failure is a particularly negative judgement about an unsuccessful work.

items.example: The comedy attracted an all-star cast for its final season.
items.note: All-star cast and star-studded cast both stress famous performers, not the quality of the script.

items.example: The opening chapter will hold your attention with its unusual narrator.
items.note: Hold someone's attention refers to maintaining interest, often over an extended narrative.

items.example: The final passage left a lasting impression on everyone in our reading group.
items.note: Make or leave a lasting impression means have an effect that remains in memory.

items.example: The performance made an indelible impression on the young musicians.
items.note: Indelible suggests an effect so powerful that it cannot easily be forgotten.

items.example: The illustrated collection will fire your imagination with its strange new worlds.
items.note: Fire someone's imagination means inspire vivid ideas or creative excitement.

items.example: A radio drama awakened an interest in local history among the students.
items.note: Awaken an interest in describes causing a new curiosity or enthusiasm to develop.

items.example: Muted colours and distant footsteps create an atmosphere of unease.
items.note: Create an atmosphere is a natural phrase for establishing an emotional mood in art.

items.example: The sparse dialogue evokes an atmosphere of isolation without explaining everything.
items.note: Evoke an atmosphere emphasises calling a particular mood to mind, rather than making it literally.

items.example: The playwright already had a considerable reputation before her first film script.
items.note: Considerable reputation is natural for an established standing; high reputation is not.

items.example: The editor earned a well-deserved reputation for discovering new voices.
items.note: Well-deserved states that a favourable reputation is justified by achievement.

items.example: A recently released film explores the friendship between two rival musicians.
items.note: Recently released identifies a new release without automatically judging its merits.

items.example: After years in television, the performer finally appeared on the big screen.
items.note: Big screen conventionally means the cinema, contrasted with television or home viewing.

units.title: Unit 30 — Regulations and authority
learningObjectives: Discuss legal obligations, workplace safety and regulatory compliance using precise formal collocations.
Distinguish seeking, granting and obtaining permission in building and administrative procedures.
Describe official authority and rule-breaking while recognising register and disparaging language.

items.example: Parliament voted to pass a new law on the handling of hazardous materials.
items.note: Pass a law describes legislative approval, not an individual's decision to obey it.

items.example: The ministry plans to introduce new regulations on laboratory waste next year.
items.note: Introduce regulations means formally establish rules; it does not mean merely explain existing ones.

items.example: The local authority will bring in regulations for commercial drone flights.
items.note: Bring in regulations is a phrasal-verb alternative to introduce regulations.

items.example: The hospital wants to standardise procedures across all its clinics.
items.note: Standardise procedures means make working methods consistent across different settings.

items.example: Every contractor must adhere to standards for electrical safety.
items.note: Adhere to is relatively formal and takes standards, rules or principles as its object.

items.example: Small businesses must comply with the law even when inspections are infrequent.
items.note: Comply with the law is a formal expression for acting in accordance with legal requirements.

items.example: Employers have an obligation to provide adequate protective equipment.
items.note: Have an obligation is more formal than have to and commonly introduces a duty with to.

items.example: Before opening the workshop, the manager will carry out a risk assessment.
items.note: Carry out a risk assessment means systematically identify and evaluate potential hazards.

items.example: The firm was found to be in breach of the law after the inspection.
items.note: In breach of the law is a formal phrase for a legal violation, often after be or find.

items.example: New barriers were installed to minimise danger to pedestrians.
items.note: Minimise danger means reduce risk as far as practicable, not necessarily eliminate it.

items.example: The redesigned platform should satisfy the requirements of the accessibility code.
items.note: Satisfy requirements means meet stipulated conditions or criteria, often in official contexts.

items.example: The organisers must seek permission before using the public square.
items.note: Seek permission is more formal than ask for permission and means request authorisation.

items.example: The council agreed to grant permission for the renovation of the old theatre.
items.note: Grant permission describes an authority giving approval to another person or organisation.

items.example: Residents must obtain permission before altering the protected building.
items.note: Obtain permission emphasises successfully receiving authorisation, rather than asking for it.

items.example: We need to put in an application before the deadline at the end of May.
items.note: Put in an application means formally submit a request; the expression is common in British English.

items.pt: licença urbanística para construir ou reformar
items.example: The owners secured planning permission for a modest extension.
items.note: Planning permission is an official approval for specified building or land-use work.

items.example: The government may introduce new legislation governing short-term rentals.
items.note: Introduce legislation describes proposing or establishing legal measures in a formal context.

items.example: Officials decided to tighten controls on industrial emissions.
items.note: Tighten controls means make restrictions or supervision more stringent.

items.example: The revised building plans must not infringe the regulations on protected sites.
items.note: Infringe regulations is a formal way to say that rules have been violated.

items.example: Residents complained about faceless bureaucrats who never explained their decisions.
items.note: Faceless bureaucrats is a disparaging expression suggesting remote, impersonal officials.

items.example: Anyone in a position of authority should explain how decisions are made.
items.note: A position of authority is a role granting power to direct or decide for others.

items.example: The inspector can exercise authority only within the powers granted by law.
items.note: Exercise authority is formal for using official power, not for receiving that power.

items.example: A single online form should help applicants cut through red tape.
items.note: Cut through red tape means overcome cumbersome administrative procedures quickly.

items.pt: impedir a execução de um plano
items.example: The planning committee voted to block a plan for the new car park.
items.note: Block a plan means obstruct or prevent a proposal from going ahead.

items.example: The company was fined for choosing to flout the rules on waste disposal.
items.note: Flout is a formal verb implying open or deliberate disregard, not an accidental mistake.

items.example: Protecting the original documents is absolutely essential during restoration.
items.note: Absolutely collocates naturally with essential; very essential is generally avoided.

items.example: The two organisations hope to reach an agreement by the end of the month.
items.note: Reach an agreement is idiomatic; get to an agreement is not the usual form.

items.example: After several rounds of talks, the partners arrived at an agreement.
items.note: Arrive at an agreement is a slightly more formal alternative to reach an agreement.

items.example: Applicants must meet the requirements listed in the safety notice.
items.note: Meet requirements is a common alternative to satisfy requirements, especially for eligibility.

items.example: The charity must satisfy conditions attached to the public grant.
items.note: Satisfy conditions often means fulfil formal terms for approval or funding.

items.example: Every participant must adhere to the rules of the competition.
items.note: Adhere to the rules is a formal alternative to follow the rules.

items.pt: agir com discricionariedade ou bom julgamento
items.example: Supervisors may exercise discretion when a deadline falls on a public holiday.
items.note: Exercise discretion means use judgement within the limits of one's authority.

items.example: University staff have a duty to report serious safety incidents.
items.note: Have a duty commonly introduces a moral, professional or legal responsibility.

items.example: The researchers carried out an experiment to compare two sensor designs.
items.note: Carry out combines naturally with experiment, assessment and investigation.

items.example: The chair declined to pass a comment on the confidential allegations.
items.note: Pass a comment is used in some contexts, but make a comment is generally more neutral and common.

items.example: The committee voted to approve a plan for improved street lighting.
items.note: Approve a plan concerns accepting a proposal; granting permission concerns allowing an action.

items.example: The panel decided not to impose a punishment for the first offence.
items.note: Impose punishment is a formal phrase for applying a sanction through authority.

items.example: The shop owner did not realise that the new practice could break the law.
items.note: Break the law is a common and less formal counterpart to be in breach of the law.

items.pt: obter licença para construir ou reformar
items.example: The builders could not start until they had obtained planning permission.
items.note: Obtain planning permission is specific to permission for building or land-use work.
